extracted.intended_audience: educational psychologists, researchers and graduate students studying emotions, measurement, and self-regulated learning
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, measuring, and researching students' academic emotions (taxonomy, scale development, and testing effects on self-regulated learning and achievement). Covers qualitative exploration, AEQ scale construction, validation, and empirical designs used to test emotion effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research questions guiding studies on academic emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Five guiding research questions: (1) Which emotions do students experience in academic settings and how are emotional experiences structured? (2) How can we measure students' academic emotions? (3) How do these emotions affect learning, achievement, and health? (4) What are the origins of these emotions within personality and environments? (5) What can we do to foster positive academic emotions and help students cope with negative emotions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These questions define the scope of inquiry and imply use of both qualitative (to explore phenomenology and generate hypotheses) and quantitative (to measure and test effects) methods. The paper focuses mainly on the first four as prerequisites for applied interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain definition: 'academic emotions'
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'academic emotions' as emotions directly linked to academic learning, classroom instruction, and achievement (e.g., enjoyment of learning, pride of success, test-related anxiety), including self-referenced, task-related, and social emotions experienced in school or university settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This domain definition delimits what emotions to measure and study (goes beyond success/failure to instruction and studying processes). It legitimizes development of domain-specific measures rather than general trait emotion scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of discrete academic emotions (target set for measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Target emotions include enjoyment, hope, pride, relief, anger, anxiety, shame, hopelessness, and boredom (the AEQ core set); broader domain also lists joy, enthusiasm, gratitude, admiration, sadness, disappointment, envy, contempt, surprise, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection criteria for the AEQ core: (a) categories of primary human emotions relevant in academic settings; (b) emotions frequently reported in exploratory studies; (c) include positive and negative, activating and deactivating emotions (valence × activation). Table 2 gives task/process/prospective/retrospective/social distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain- and situation-specific scales (class-related, learning-related, test-related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct separate scales pertaining to class-related, learning-related, and test-related emotions to reflect differences in functions and social structure of situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items should be developed and administered with instructions tailored to the situation (e.g., in-class experience vs. studying vs. exam). This supports better predictive validity than general trait emotion measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-dimensional conceptual framework: valence and activation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptualize emotions along two primary dimensions — valence (positive vs. negative) and activation (activating vs. deactivating) — as basic determinants of emotion effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these dimensions to classify emotions and predict differing effects on motivation, strategies, cognitive resources, and achievement. Recognize simplifications and exceptions (e.g., anxiety may freeze behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four emotion groups derived from valence × activation
rubrics_metrics.description: Group emotions into: (a) positive activating (e.g., enjoyment, hope, pride), (b) positive deactivating (e.g., relief), (c) negative activating (e.g., anger, anxiety, shame), and (d) negative deactivating (e.g., boredom, hopelessness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use group membership to hypothesize differential effects: positive activating generally enhance motivation and flexible learning; negative deactivating generally detrimental; positive deactivating and negative activating may have ambivalent effects depending on context and task demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Component-process model for emotion item content
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat emotions as sets of interrelated psychological processes — affective, cognitive, physiological, and motivational components — and reflect these components in item content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include items covering feelings (affect), thoughts (cognitions), bodily activation (physiology), and action tendencies/goals (motivation). Different emotions may show differing internal component structure; some scales separate components while others show less differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use qualitative exploratory data to inform item construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive item content from qualitative interviews and reports about students' emotional episodes to capture phenomenology and component profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative exploration helps detect unexpected phenomena (e.g., meta-emotions, varied causes of boredom) and supplies empirically grounded item pools for subsequent quantitative scale construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item construction and selection procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with an initial item pool from qualitative data and theory; use expert judgment and redundancy criteria to form preliminary scales; select final items based on item statistics and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow iterative selection: eliminate redundant or poorly performing items using psychometric analysis; use CFA to confirm scale structures and component separation where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-item measurement per emotion (avoid single-item scales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple items for each emotion to represent different components and improve reliability rather than single-item ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-item scales better capture internal structures and yield acceptable reliability; single-item measures may be economical but lack reliability and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmatory factor analysis for structure validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use CFA to evaluate the internal structure of each emotion scale (components, factor separations, and scale dimensionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFA revealed that affective, cognitive, physiological, and motivational components separated in some scales (e.g., test anxiety) but not in others (e.g., boredom). Use CFA results to refine scales and interpret component overlaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability standards for AEQ scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Target internal consistencies (Cronbach's alpha) in the range reported: approximately .84–.94 for long trait and state scales; short and translated versions with average reliabilities around .86–.87.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 3 reports scale alphas and item counts; aim for similar reliability levels. Provide both long and short versions; verify reliabilities across trait/course/state versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide trait, course-related, and state versions and short forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct scales so they can be administered as trait measures, course-specific (course-related) measures, or state measures; additionally provide shorter (e.g., eight-item) versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design items and instructions to allow flexibility; short forms should preserve adequate reliability for applied contexts; verify equivalence of reliability and validity across versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address discriminant validity and item overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that some items/components may be shared across emotions (e.g., worry items in test anxiety scales may tap shame or hopelessness), complicating discriminant validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret scale correlations cautiously; use CFA and careful item wording to reduce cross-loading; consider theoretical and empirical justifications for keeping highly correlated scales separate (e.g., anxiety vs hopelessness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure interrelations and cluster emotions empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze correlations among emotion scales to identify clusters (e.g., enjoyment/hope/pride; relief; anxiety/shame/hopelessness; anger/boredom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clusters can suggest shared antecedents and effects; examine both within-cluster and between-cluster correlations and their implications for hierarchical models of affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple research designs: cross-sectional, longitudinal, diary
rubrics_metrics.description: Test theoretical assumptions using a combination of designs: cross-sectional studies for associations, longitudinal studies for reciprocal causation, and diary methods for idiographic and state-level dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program used 7 cross-sectional, 3 longitudinal, and 1 diary study; different designs answer different causal and temporal questions—use them complementarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include behavioral and physiological validation measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Complement self-reports with physiological measures (e.g., cortisol, physiological activation) and behavioral/observational data where possible to validate self-reported emotion intensity and coping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative reports of emotional intensity were systematically related to cortisol; questionnaire-based measures showed less consistent physiological relations. Combine methods to strengthen inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select criterion/outcome measures for effects on self-regulated learning
rubrics_metrics.description: When testing emotion effects, measure motivation, learning strategies (elaboration, rehearsal, monitoring), cognitive resources (task-irrelevant thinking), regulation (self-regulated vs external regulation), effort, and academic achievement (grades, exam performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established scales (e.g., Study Interest Scale, MSLQ adaptations) and objective achievement indicators; analyze mediating pathways (motivation, strategies, resources) linking emotions to achievement (see Table 4 for exemplary correlations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesize mediating mechanisms (cognitive-motivational model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume that emotions affect achievement through mediators: motivation, learning strategies, cognitive resources, and self-regulation, with different emotions influencing these mediators in different ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the valence × activation classification to derive predictions (e.g., positive activating enhances flexible strategies; negative deactivating reduces motivation and superficial processing). Test mediated pathways empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider ambivalent and context-dependent emotion effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that some emotions (especially negative-activating and positive-deactivating) may have mixed effects depending on expectancies, task demands, and the need for cognitive flexibility versus algorithmic procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic assumptions that positive = good and negative = bad. For example, anxiety may impair complex tasks but motivate effort on rote tasks; relief may reduce immediate motivation but reinforce long-term effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design scales to permit temporal generality and instruction variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct items so they can be administered under different instructions to measure trait, course-related, or state emotions (temporal and situational generality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows comparison across trait/state and adaptation of items for specific courses or single episodes; verify measurement invariance across instruction sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use expert judgment and redundancy criteria in preliminary item pruning
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply content-expert review and redundancy checks to reduce initial item pools before empirical item analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This step streamlines subsequent psychometric testing and ensures content coverage while removing duplicate items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and report cross-linguistic and contextual equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating scales (e.g., German → English) or applying them in different educational contexts (school vs. university; subject domains), evaluate reliability and validity equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The English-language short AEQ versions showed average reliability ≈ .86; develop domain-specific school versions (e.g., for mathematics) and test psychometric properties in each context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate analysis of coping and emotional regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure coping strategies and emotion regulation processes as they relate to physiological activation and performance (e.g., problem-focused and emotion-oriented coping related to lower cortisol).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying coping/ regulation helps explain functional relations between subjective emotions and physiological responses and may identify intervention targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance sample-based designs with idiographic analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Complement sample-average (nomothetic) studies with idiographic (within-person) designs to ascertain generalizability to individual students and reduce artefacts of sample statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diary and time-series methods can capture individual dynamics and provide insight into within-person feedback loops between emotions and achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for reciprocal causation and feedback loops in longitudinal models
rubrics_metrics.description: Model bidirectional influences (e.g., achievement ↔ test anxiety) using longitudinal data to identify positive and negative feedback loops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longitudinal analyses in Grades 5–10 showed reciprocal effects; simple cross-sectional correlations may obscure these dynamics—use appropriate longitudinal modeling techniques.
